Will you get a 1099-K this year?

A private checker for gig and marketplace sellers (eBay, Etsy, Poshmark, Venmo, PayPal, Cash App, StockX, and others). The federal reporting threshold has changed four times since 2022 — enter what a platform paid you and get a per-platform answer against the right year's figure, plus four states' own stricter rule.

After using this, you can now see which of your platforms are likely to send a 1099-K and which are not, per platform and per year, which used to mean re-deriving four years of threshold whiplash by hand. See the full threshold timeline explained, or how this compares to checking it yourself.

Already have a 1099-K in hand and want to know what it means for your taxable profit — backing out refunds, fees, and cost of goods? The 1099-K reconciliation worksheet handles that side of the same question — nothing uploaded there either.

Selling on platforms in the EU instead? The EU equivalent is DAC7: the DAC7 seller reporting checker shows whether a platform will report your sales to the tax authority.

Selling into several states, not just several platforms? A 1099-K is about payment reporting, not sales tax — the economic nexus threshold tracker answers the separate question of which states you may owe sales tax registration in.

Tax year

Add a platform

Each platform is checked on its own — amounts from different platforms are never added together, because that is not how the threshold works.

Platform names and amounts stay on this device. Nothing is uploaded. Usage counts contain only feature names and are never sent anywhere.

Common questions

What is the 1099-K threshold for 2026?

More than $20,000 in gross payments and more than 200 transactions from the same platform in the year. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA, signed 2025-07-04) restored this figure after a since-repealed law would have phased it down to $600. Both conditions must be exceeded — a platform that paid you $25,000 across 50 transactions has not crossed the federal threshold.

Why did my platform send me a 1099-K for 2024 when I made less than $20,000?

For tax year 2024 specifically, the IRS had announced a real $5,000 threshold with no transaction-count minimum (Notice 2023-74), and platforms actually issued forms under it. The 2025 law that restored $20,000/200 going forward applies retroactively to 2024 too, but the IRS confirmed a platform that already sent a 2024 form under the $5,000 rule did not have to withdraw or correct it — so a form that already arrived for 2024 stays valid even though the current standing threshold is higher.

Do amounts from different platforms add together?

No. The threshold applies separately to each Third Party Settlement Organization (TPSO) — each marketplace or payment app checks its own total paid to you, on its own. $15,000 from eBay and $15,000 from Etsy in the same year does not combine into $30,000 for either platform's own reporting decision. Enter each platform as its own row.

I'm under the threshold everywhere. Does that mean I owe no tax on this income?

No. Whether a 1099-K is issued and whether the income is taxable are two separate questions. Business income is reportable whether or not any form documents it. This checker only estimates the paperwork question — it is not tax advice about what to report.

Does crossing the threshold guarantee a form arrives, or does staying under it guarantee one will not?

Neither is guaranteed. A platform can choose to issue a 1099-K below the federal or state threshold (some do, for internal reasons or backup withholding), and a platform that should issue one can still make a filing error. This tool estimates the legal threshold, not any specific platform's actual behavior.

My state isn't Maryland, Massachusetts, Vermont, or Virginia. Does it have its own threshold?

Possibly, but this tool has not independently verified all fifty states' own reporting statutes — only these four, which are confirmed to set a threshold stricter than the federal one. If your state is not listed, this checker applies the federal threshold only; check your state's own department of revenue if you want to rule out a state-specific rule.

No warranty. This tool is free and as-is. It is not legal, financial, or tax advice, and it does not know what any specific platform actually did or will do. It is not the IRS TIN Matching program, and it does not file anything. A "likely" or "unlikely" estimate is a starting point for your own review, not a determination. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Free and open source. If it saved you from an unpleasant surprise in January, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

This checker vs. looking up the 1099-K threshold yourself

Figuring out whether a marketplace or payment app is likely to send you a Form 1099-K is arithmetic anyone can do — if they have the right figure. The problem is that the right figure depends on the tax year, sometimes on your state, and always on treating each platform separately, and a quick manual check often misses one of those without any sign that something was skipped.

Where a manual check usually goes wrong

StepCommon mistake looking it up yourselfWhat this checker does
Picking the right year's figureUsing whatever number a search result or old bookmark shows, which may be last year's transition-relief figure ($5,000 for 2024 only) instead of the current $20,000/200 standing rule, or vice versa.Applies the correct federal figure for the exact tax year you enter, and shows a note when that year had a one-off wrinkle (2024).
Reading "exceeds" vs. "at least"Rounding "exceeds $20,000 and exceeds 200 transactions" up to "at least," which gets a seller sitting at exactly $20,000 across exactly 200 transactions the wrong answer.Applies the IRS's own strictly-greater-than wording every time, with no rounding.
Combining platformsAdding up what every platform paid you before comparing to the threshold, when the rule applies per platform, not to your total marketplace income.Checks each platform you enter on its own, against its own total.
Checking for a state overrideNot knowing that Maryland, Massachusetts, Vermont, and Virginia each set their own $600 threshold, independent of the federal figure and easy to miss if you only check the federal rule.Applies each of those four states' own stricter threshold automatically when you select your state, on top of the federal check.
Is anything I enter uploaded anywhere?N/ANo. The checker runs entirely in your browser; nothing you enter is sent to a server.

Common questions

What's the most common mistake when looking up the 1099-K threshold yourself?

Using last year's figure. The federal threshold has changed four times since 2022: $20,000/200 transactions through 2023, $5,000 with no transaction minimum for 2024 only, then back to $20,000/200 from 2025 on. A search result, a news article, or even an old bookmark can easily be reporting a figure that applied to a different tax year than the one you're checking.

Why does it matter whether the threshold is "at least" or "exceeds"?

Because they produce opposite answers at the boundary. The IRS's own wording is "exceeds $20,000" and "exceeds 200 transactions" — strictly greater than, not "at least." A seller paid exactly $20,000 across exactly 200 transactions has not crossed the federal threshold under either condition. A quick mental check that rounds "exceeds" up to "at least" gets this specific case wrong.

Do I need to add up what every platform paid me before checking the threshold?

No — and this is the mistake most likely to produce a wrong answer for someone selling on several platforms. The threshold applies separately to each Third Party Settlement Organization (TPSO). $15,000 from eBay and $15,000 from Etsy in the same year does not combine into $30,000 for either platform's own reporting decision; each platform checks only what it itself paid you.

How would I know if my state has a stricter threshold than the federal one?

Only four states currently do: Maryland, Massachusetts, Vermont, and Virginia, each at $600 with no transaction-count minimum, independent of whichever federal figure applies that year. That is not the kind of fact most people carry into a manual check, and a state's own department-of-revenue page is easy to overlook if you're only checking the federal rule.

If I check by hand and land on the wrong side of the threshold, what actually happens?

Nothing about the actual law changes either way — a platform still applies its own reporting obligation regardless of what you calculated. What changes is whether you're caught off guard: expecting no form and getting one in January, or assuming a form means taxable income was newly created when it was always reportable. Getting the estimate right ahead of time is about avoiding the surprise, not the obligation.

No warranty. This page and the linked checker apply the federal and four state 1099-K thresholds to numbers you supply. It is not tax, legal, or financial advice, is not the IRS TIN Matching program, and does not know what any specific platform actually did or will do. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. The checker this page links to runs entirely client-side; nothing you enter is uploaded anywhere.

why-did-the-1099-k-threshold-keep-changi.text:
← 1099-K Threshold Checker

Why did the 1099-K threshold keep changing?

Four different numbers have governed Form 1099-K since 2022, and the platforms that follow them did not all move in lockstep. Here is the full timeline, in order, and why a form that already arrived for 2024 can look inconsistent with what the rule says today.

Open the free 1099-K threshold checker

The timeline

Tax yearThreshold platforms actually usedWhy
2011–2021$20,000, more than 200 transactionsThe original rule
2022$20,000, more than 200 transactionsARPA's $600 figure was delayed by IRS notice before it took effect
2023$20,000, more than 200 transactionsDelayed again by a second IRS notice
2024$5,000, no transaction-count minimumA real transition threshold (Notice 2023-74), actually used to issue forms
2025 and later$20,000, more than 200 transactionsOBBBA repealed ARPA's threshold before the planned $2,500-for-2025 step took effect

The 2024 wrinkle

The IRS's October 2025 Fact Sheet 2025-08 confirmed that OBBBA's restoration of $20,000/200 applies retroactively back to the 2022 tax year — meaning the law now treats $20,000/200 as having technically applied even in 2024. But that retroactive correction did not undo what platforms had already done: a platform that issued a 2024 Form 1099-K under the real $5,000 threshold in effect at the time did not have to withdraw or correct it, and one that stayed silent under the old $600 assumption faced no penalty either way.

So if you received a 1099-K for 2024 on payments between $5,000 and $20,000, that form is not a mistake — it reflects the rule that was actually in force when it was issued, even though the standing rule today is higher. This checker asks for the platform's actual threshold for the year you are checking, rather than only the current legal figure, so a past-year question gets an answer that matches what really happened.

What stayed the same throughout

The threshold applies per platform, never combined across the different apps and marketplaces you use. And meeting or missing a threshold has never changed whether the underlying income is taxable — a 1099-K is paperwork about payments already received, not the event that makes them reportable.

Common questions

What was the 1099-K threshold before 2022?

$20,000 in gross payments and more than 200 transactions, both required, from 2011 through 2021. That is also the current threshold — the number spent three years lower and then came back.

What changed in 2022?

The American Rescue Plan Act (ARPA), passed in 2021, legislated a much lower $600 threshold with no transaction-count minimum, intended to take effect for the 2022 tax year. The IRS delayed enforcement of that lower figure by notice, first for 2022 and then again for 2023, so platforms kept using $20,000/200 in practice for both years even though the statute on the books said $600.

What actually happened in 2024?

The IRS announced a real transition threshold of $5,000, with no transaction-count minimum, as a step toward the eventual $600 figure (Notice 2023-74). This one was not delayed — platforms actually issued Form 1099-K under the $5,000 rule for payments made in 2024, filed in early 2025.

What happened for 2025 and after?

The next planned step was $2,500 for 2025, on the way down to $600 for 2026. Before that lower 2025 figure ever took effect, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), signed 2025-07-04, repealed ARPA's threshold entirely and restored $20,000/200 transactions. The IRS's Fact Sheet 2025-08 (October 2025) confirmed this applies retroactively back to the 2022 tax year — so the $600 and $2,500 figures never actually took legal effect for any year, and $20,000/200 is the standing rule for 2025, 2026, and beyond.

If the law now says $20,000 applied to 2024 too, does that undo the 1099-K I already got for 2024?

No. The IRS confirmed that a platform that already issued a 2024 Form 1099-K under the real $5,000 rule that was in effect at the time did not have to withdraw or correct it, and a platform that did not issue one under that rule faces no penalty either way. The retroactive correction changes what the standing legal threshold is considered to have been; it does not reach back and cancel a form that already arrived in your mailbox.

No warranty. This page is not legal, financial, or tax advice. Verify the current figures against the IRS's own Form 1099-K FAQs or your tax preparer before relying on any number here.
